title: Largest US Grid Operator Proposes Shutting Off Data Centers During Power Crunches
excerpt: PJM Interconnection, which serves 67 million people across 13 states, would curtail electricity to data centers 50MW and larger during grid emergencies starting June 2027.
body:
• PJM Interconnection, the largest U.S. grid operator serving 67 million people across 13 states, has proposed temporarily shutting off electricity to large data centers during grid emergencies to prevent rolling blackouts.
  • The plan, filed with federal regulators, would take effect in June 2027 and target facilities of 50 megawatts or larger that do not supply their own power generation.
  • PJM's recent capacity auction fell short by 6.8 gigawatts, as surging data center demand outpaces new power plant construction and threatens to push costs onto residential consumers.

The operator of the largest electrical grid in the United States has proposed a stark ultimatum for data centers: bring your own power, or risk having the lights turned off.

PJM Interconnection, which manages electricity for 67 million people in a territory stretching from Washington, D.C., to Chicago across 13 states, filed a proposal with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on August 13 that would allow it to temporarily curtail electricity to large data centers during periods of extreme grid stress. The plan would take effect in June 2027.

A 6.8-Gigawatt Shortfall

The proposal follows a capacity auction in which PJM fell short of its reliability requirement by approximately 6.8 gigawatts — enough to power roughly five million homes. Despite power prices hitting a cap of $325 per megawatt-day, meant to incentivize new plant construction, the grid operator could not attract sufficient generating resources to meet projected demand.

https://x.com/Mayhem4Markets/status/2089489235145322666

That shortfall raises the risk of blackouts across PJM's territory, which includes Virginia — home to the world's largest concentration of data centers — along with parts of Illinois, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

PJM forecasts that new large loads, primarily driven by data centers, will increase by an estimated 70 gigawatts by 2038, while some 15 gigawatts of generating capacity have retired since 2022.

"PJM's proposal marks a significant shift by making electricity access conditional for some large new data centers during grid emergencies."

— Pareekh Jain, CEO, EIIRTrend & Pareekh Consulting

Protecting Residential Ratepayers

The plan specifically targets data centers and other facilities with cumulative peak load of at least 50 megawatts at a single site. Under the proposal, those that do not bring their own generation or otherwise secure independent supply would be subject to curtailment before PJM deploys its existing emergency load management programs.

PJM said its proposals seek to protect residential customers from paying higher energy prices driven by data center expansion. Over the past year, wholesale electricity prices in PJM's territory have nearly doubled, and the grid operator's independent market monitor has blamed data centers for much of the increase. Capacity prices have soared more than 1,000 percent since roughly 2024.

The grid operator also proposed creating a Large Load Registry to track the location and electricity consumption of data centers and other major users.

Industry Pushback and Backup Plans

The proposal has drawn criticism from multiple directions. Big Tech companies are not enthusiastic about the prospect of disconnection during peak demand, but industry observers say hyperscalers may have little choice if they want faster grid connections.

The move is likely to spur many data centers to set up their own on-site power sources. Those that do not will probably rely on backup diesel generators, which are costlier to operate and frequently more polluting. Federal regulations allow such generators to be used for up to 50 hours per year for demand response events.

PJM does not currently have the authority to curtail power to data centers unilaterally and would require cooperation from individual state governments. The Department of Energy has already granted PJM emergency authorization during recent extreme weather events, directing local utilities to order data centers to use backup power during grid emergencies.

A Political Headache

Rapid data center growth has become politically contentious in PJM's territory. A growing number of residents fear they will be saddled with rising costs to provide power to data center complexes they view as noisy and intrusive. The tension highlights a fundamental question in the AI boom: who pays when the infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence strains the grid that powers everything else.
